886054,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.2.1,1929-06-12,f0d1049a-4acc-4789-a93f-b3bceae69e3f,ca.m.8624,Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (Wetaskiwin):,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,,,"Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the house for a very few minutes to a question of considerable importance, at least to working men. I ask the government to consider the desirability of opening the parliamentary session at a different time of the year from that which is now the practice. I do not know whether the month of February was selected to inconvenience western members as much as possible, particularly farmer members, but were that the purpose it has been very well executed. It is the custom for parliament to meet in February, or perhaps even later. As a result we are now in the summer months roasting and frying in this building, when we ought to be out in the sunshine storing up health, especially when we have to stay indoors so long during the winter months. Surely the time is come for us to consider whether February is the best time for parliament to meet.
It goes without saying that seed time is one of great importance to the farmer mem-

bers, and it also goes without saying that the members coming from the maritime provinces on the one hand and from British Columbia and the western provinces on the other have to stay here steadily throughout the session; they have no opportunity of going home over the week end or during a short adjournment; and to have to remain in Ottawa during the spring season when they ought to be at their work at home imposes on them a very serious inconvenience. I believe it would be better for all concerned were parliament to meet two or three months earlier than it usually does. I think November would be a very excellent time to open the session, have a recess for Christmas and New Year, and then come back and conclude our parliamentary work before the first of May at least.

That is the suggestion I wish to make. It may be that some members from the eastern provinces would rather continue the present practice, but I think they ought to be prepared to give a little consideration to this suggestion, since the change would involve no inconvenience to any one, whereas if we continue to meet in February western members are very seriously inconvenienced.

There is a further reason why I think eastern members ought to give favourable consideration to my plea. I think it is clear to any one who looks at the matter from the point of view of indemnities that the western members are discriminated against. No man can be here steadily for four months and attend to any kind of personal business. He has practically to give it up. That is true also of the maritime members. I do not know whether one should mention the word ""indemnity"" or not. Far be it from me to suggest any increase!

,United Farmers of Alberta,,William Irvine,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f0d1049a-4acc-4789-a93f-b3bceae69e3f&Language=E&Section=ALL

,,,Some hon. MEMBERS:,
886056,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.2.3,1929-06-12,f0d1049a-4acc-4789-a93f-b3bceae69e3f,ca.m.8624,Mr. IRVINE:,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,,,I would not think of making such a suggestion. I know that all parties are very much afraid of this question, especially the leaders. I might go so far as to suggest that $1,000 be taken off the indemnity of the eastern members and added to that of the western members. This would not increase the taxation in any way, while it would make up some of the difference which now exists as between eastern and western members. It is clear I think that eastern members have a little advantage over those from .the west, and if $4,000 be a reasonable indemnity for a man who can be in his office every day in the year it is very unfair to a member from Vancouver or from any of the western provinces. Even if for some minor reason eastern members would rather be here

in the spring of the year, I submit that in view of all the circumstances they ought to be prepared to assist us in our effort to impress upon the government the advisability of changing the time at which parliament meets, making it November instead of February.

In conclusion, I wish to say this. There is a great deal more in the suggestion than may appear on the surface, for the question of indemnity is one which leads us to another question of moment to the people of Canada and to the democratic system in general. I believe that it is becoming more and more the tendency that only rich men can come to this parliament; and poor men, however able they may be, may ultimately be debarred except they may possibly receive assistance from some other source to enable them to attend parliament-which is perhaps a principle equally as dangerous as the principle of having only rich men in parliament. And there is a tendency in Canada for that principle to take root. I think we can find instances, without going back very far, of outstanding men of the main parties in Canada who have been assisted or indemnified by private persons-we do not know who they are- in order that they might be in a position to give their services to the country. Now I offer no criticism of any individual; I do not know any case in which this has been done [DOT]wherein the individual concerned was not an outstanding man whose services Canada could ill afford to lose, and of which we are very glad to have had the benefit. That is not my criticism, however; my criticism is that the principle is a very bad one. At least we ought to know in every case who the men are that subscribe funds, and I would rather advocate that Canada be prepared to give, to those whose services the country accepts, a remuneration sufficient to maintain them, having full control over them, than prejudice their services by allowing private individuals to keep them in public life.

I hope that in view of all the circumstances the government will listen to our request that parliament meet in the fall instead of in the spring, and that we be careful not to allow mere wealth to supersede other qualities in this parliament. I frankly admit, of course, that I should be very glad indeed if I had sufficient political influence to be worth $200,000 to anybody outside parliament. Unfortunately, however, I am not in that happy position and so I stand for the democratic principle of having the people of Canada pay the services of their representatives. And if it were necessary I would even suggest that the personnel of parliament be reduced by 78594-228

half, paying the memtiers an adequate compensation, and applying the same principle to ministers, reducing their number to the same extent and adequately remunerating them in order to keep in public life men whose services are of value to the country.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.

would be just as well to discuss it under this item, 'because I have one or two remarks to make in connection with the statement made to the house by the right hon. the Prime Minister, when speaking on the budget. I want to get this matter straightened out because, in my judgment, the statement made by the Prime Minister was very misleading and not at all in accordance with the facts. I take it that the funded debt of Canada on March 31, 1922, was $2,420,000,000, in round figures, and1 according to the Canadian Gazette of April 13, I find that the funded debt of Canada on March 31, 1929, was $2,363,000,000. It will be understood that I am giving round figures. When I was speaking on the budget I gave the funded debt of Canada as of March 31 last as being $2,330,000,000, so it would appear that I was just $33,000,000 too low. I obtained those figures in the course of conversation a day or -two before with the Minister of Finance. When I stated that there had been a reduction in seven years of $90,000,000 in the funded debt of Canada, I should have stated that there had been a reduction of $57,000,000. The right hon. the Prime Minister made what to my mind is the most ridiculous financial statement which has ever been made in the House of Commons. The right hon. the Prime Minister said that I had overlooked entirely the fact that in 1922 there was a floating debt of $144,000,000, and that this government had paid that floating debt because it had disappeared. According to the statement of 1922 there were against that funded debt assets which have also disappeared from the public accounts of Canada. Schedule B of the public accounts for 1922, shows the following assets as appearing on the balance sheet of Canada and which are carried as cash:

The minister stated that the government had paid $144,000,000 of floating debt, but I ask him where these assets have gone. According to the statement which appears in the Canada Gazette, the assets amount to $31,049,000, while in March, 1922, they amounted to $162,766,000. What has become of those assets, cash assets which were carried on the balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada? Those assets h&ve been liquidated and the money has been used to pay the floating debt of $144,000,000. The assets are gone and the floating debt is gone, and the balance has not been affected at all.

The right hon. the Prime Minister knew that fact when he made his speech, or if he did not know he should have known. I submitted those figures to an accountant and I was told that a more ridiculous proposition had never been put up to him in all his experience. If the assets were still there then I could understand that the debt had been paid, but that debt was paid out of the cash assets. The money had been borrowed from the banks to advance to these foreign governments, and when that was paid the money was repaid to the banks and the balance of the Dominion of Canada was not affected at all. When I stated that in seven years the Minister of Finance had reduced the funded debt by $90,000,000, I was giving him credit for $33,000,000 too much; the amount should have been $57,000,000 and not $90,000,000. I cannot say who supplied this information to the Minister of Finance, but if it was a member of the Finance department, that man should be hauled over the coals and brought before the Auditor General because he does not know his business.

The work the girl guides are doing is of first importance to Canada, and I think it worth while to place on record an incident that happened not very long ago in Winnipeg, where the girl guides were the means of saving life. Perhaps this may be of interest to the Canadian Press Association, because one of the girls was the daughter of a former member of the association. Three girls were playing on the street. Another girl hastened up to them, spoke very hurriedly, and they followed her. They found a man being suffocated in a garage. They pulled him out and sent one of their number for a doctor, and in the meantime they saved the man's life by the use of artificial respiration. I thought it well to delay the house to record such an incident, for it shows the very valuable work the girl guides and boy scouts are doing for Canada.

the statement:

The covenant of the League of Nations origin-provided that the expenses of the league should be apportioned among the members on the same basis as that adopted for the expenses of the Universal Postal Union. This was found to be inequitable and an amendment to the covenant was adopted in 1924 providing that the expenses should be borne in the proportion decided by the assembly. The basis to be adopted has been considered by committees of various assemblies. The question of the weight to be given to such factors as national revenue, population, trade returns depreciation of currency, was repeatedly considered. A scale of allocation was adopted by the assembly in 1926, and the ninth assembly voted to continue on that basis until 1932, when it will be reconsidered.

886264,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.3.206,1929-06-12,733cae8a-7e57-46c6-ab2e-478ac991835f,ca.m.4942,Mr. LEMIEUX:,Speaker of the House of Commons,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE,,The right hon. gentleman will remember that I visited the battlefields and the memorial of Vimy in October last year. The work has progressed satisfactorily, but the committee has had considerable trouble in obtaining the proper quality of granite. Various quarries in France, Belgium, England and Scotland were inspected, when an old quarry, dating from the days of the Roman empire, was discovered in Jugoslavia, and granite of a very fine grain is being taken from there to Vimy. The foundation for the monument has been completed, and the two majestic pylons are now under construction. The surroundings of the monument are completed and also the inscription of the names of the soldiers. From what I gathered at the last sitting of the commission, and from what I heard at Vimy when I was there last fall, I believe it will take about a year and a half from the present date to complete the monument. I must say that the commission was very fortunate in having Brigadier-General Hughes as an engineer. He discovered right in front of the memorial the trenches which were used alternately by the Germans and the Allies. He has completely reconstituted these trenches, so much so that every Sunday from all parts of France, Belgium, England and even Germany, many congregate there to see our monument and also to see those historic trenches, where on the walls can be read the names of the occupants whether they were Germans or British. I can assure the committee that it is a most impressive eight. I was told that no less than

column2: to 5,000 visitors went there every Sunday during the summer and fall. As regards the beauty of the monument, it is admitted to-day by the Societe des Architectes in France, that it will be the most imposing memorial on the battlefields of Europe.

not be done without amending the British North America Act, is it the intention of the government to ask the opinion of the provinces in this respect?

886343,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.36,1929-06-12,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,Perhaps I might

give an instance of what I have in mind, although I will not mention the names of any judges; it is the principle rather than the individual that concerns me. A certain justice, dismissing from the jury a man who had intimated that for conscientious reasons he could not serve in a trial involving capital punishment, remarked that a man who adopted that attitude was not a good Canadian citizen. He is reported thus:

You have no right to live under the British flag"", said His Lordship. ""As long as the law provides for capital punishment it must be obeyed. There is a constitutional method of changing the law but it is not for jurymen to alter it.""
It does seem to me hardly the thing for a judge to take such a position when a man on conscientious grounds declares his unwilling-
ness to serve on the jury in a particular case; this man had every right to decline to act on that jury. Is there no way by which judges may be checked in rather reckless statements of this sort?

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL
886344,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.37,1929-06-12,4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c,ca.m.491,Mr. LAPOINTE:,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,My hon. friend's principle is wrong; I would not agree with him. I consider the independence of the judiciary the best safeguard of society. If we could exercise some influence on judges, I believe that everyone would suffer in Canada. The law has seen to it that our judges shall be absolutely independent of any influence whatsoever, and were a judge to take that stand again I should support him.

,Liberal,,Ernest Lapointe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c&Language=E&Section=ALL
886345,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.38,1929-06-12,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,I too wish the
judges to be independent, but not arbitrary. Let me cite another instance which has been brought to my notice. A judge addressing a prisoner said:

The jury have found you not guilty on evidence upon which a verdict of guilty might equally have been returned. For myself, I think that you fired the shot that killed. . . . and I think some steps will have to he taken. I will make my report accordingly, for I think you are not a safe man to be at large.

I do not know all the circumstances, but it seems to me very strange for the judge in this case to have swept aside the verdict of the jury. I am not a lawyer, but I regard it as an arbitrary act on the part of the judge when he undertakes to give his own opinion in this way, virtually disregarding the verdict of the jury. I should like to know whether there is any way of criticizing judges or of exercising some supervisory power, without of course, necessarily involving impeachment.

,Labour,,James Shaver Woodsworth,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916&Language=E&Section=ALL

The rules of the house forbid such criticism. So far as I am concerned, I will certainly not express my personal views as to whether the judge was right or wrong in that respect.

886347,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.40,1929-06-12,c2394337-f8ed-4555-877d-cc6d79e6700e,ca.m.5981,Mr. EVANS:,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,To emphasize the importance of the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Woods-worth), I cannot do better than give an instance that has come to my attention. In one case a car was stolen and afterwards left outside the city in a damaged condition for the owner to get it. The culprit, a lad of eighteen, was let out on suspended sentence, and during that suspension he committed four
Supply-Justice

other crimes. Altogether he was up for nine crimes, and during the course of his operations he secured booty to the extent of some $500, going so far as even to rob women; he did 'his looting at ladies' aid meetings and so forth. Nine offences were proved against him and still he was left at large on suspended sentence. He was also allowed to go into a neighbouring town to work, and apparently nothing could keep him in the right path. It seems to me that there is an utter discrimination in the dispensing of justice in the west to-day. I could mention cases to show that sentences have been unduly severe while in this particular instance I have cited it has been the very opposite.

column2: I should like to ask

column1: the minister what is the custom in the case of a vacant judgeship in one of the provinces; is an appointment made as a rule without much delay, or at times is the appointment delayed because of some doubt as to the necessity of having so many judges? I have a case in mind in my own province; I have had many requests from different gentlemen as to that appointment, and I understand that the appointment is not being made at present because there is some doubt as to whether there is enough work to necessitate the full complement of judges. I should like to know if that is the case.

friend is referring to the vacancy in the Stettler district. The reason why this vacancy has not been filled is because I have received communications from the Attorney General of Alberta saying that it might be better not to fill the vacancy owing to the work not being heavy enough to justify it. I have communicated further with him and he rather suggests that this district should be looked after by one of the other judges and that more good would be done by the appointment of a permanent judge in another district which has no resident judge at present; I think that is the Peace River district. However, the matter stands there, and we will have to reach a decision on this question. I am making investigations of my own and I will try to meet the wishes of the authorities of the province.

886392,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.85,1929-06-12,1d6a8f18-7d15-4909-b0f5-88f9b514f20a,ca.m.1201,Miss MACPHAIL:,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,I suppose she has good sense and wants to get him as far away as possible. I would like to mention the case of a prisoner who was sent from Portsmouth to Stony Mountain some time after 1925; I do not know the exact date, but he was sent to Stony Mountain and his first duties were indoor, assisting the schoolmaster and then in the tailor shop. He was then transferred and put at work in the quarry. This man wrote a letter to his mother and father in which he said:
The warden has no use for me because I complained about my work being dangerous and threatened to notify the superintendent about it.

A short time after the parents received that letter they received news of their son's death. The letter was smuggled out by a prisoner who had served his term, but it is an authentic letter. The fact that he used the words which I have just put on Hansard, followed by his death, seems to me to be a very odd coincidence. The wife and parents of this man asked the Minister of Justice to make an investigation to see whether or not he was killed because of negligence. I have received a letter from his mother and from his wife, and the mother says:
The condition of his body was shameful. He had not been embalmed.
Supply-Justice
The wife said the same thing, and in referring to the warden she also said:
I do not believe what he said because he said that the body was embalmed and we know it was not.

I think we should have information as to whether or not this man was put at dangerous work. The fact that he thought the work was dangerous and that he was killed shortly afterwards would need a careful explanation, and I would like to hear what the minister has to say about it.

,Progressive,,Agnes Campbell Macphail,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1d6a8f18-7d15-4909-b0f5-88f9b514f20a&Language=E&Section=ALL

886395,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.88,1929-06-12,4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c,ca.m.491,Mr. LAPOINTE:,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,The accident was not

caused through any defect in the machinery, and the coroner did not think it necessary to hold an investigation. This man, as well as the other convicts, had been warned not to push the stones with his hand when they were being raised by the derrick, and I have the statements of convicts, as well as of guards, to that effect. We were notified immediately by the warden of the penitentiary as to this accident and upon the request of the relatives in Toronto we instructed the warden to have the body embalmed and sent to Toronto. That was done, and it is certainly not according to the facts to state that the body was not properly embalmed, because not only have I the statement of the warden that it was, but we have paid the bill of the undertakers and the embalmers. We have a population in the penitentiaries of Canada of 2,809 and it is remarkable how few accidents happen. I think we can safely say that in no industrial plant anywhere do so few accidents occur as in the penitentiary. As I informed the hon. member, the authorities of the penitentiary sympathize with the family of the convict, but what took place is one of those things that cannot be avoided.

,Liberal,,Ernest Lapointe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c&Language=E&Section=ALL
886396,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.89,1929-06-12,1d6a8f18-7d15-4909-b0f5-88f9b514f20a,ca.m.1201,Miss MACPHAIL:,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,I am not sure that proves anything in the world, because the warden certainly is not going to say that this was carelessness on his part, and I will guarantee that the guards and the prisoners dare not say so. As regards the sworn statement of the prisoner, if the warden is to blame, that statement would not be worth the trouble of writing it or the paper it was written on. These men are absolutely under his command and I am convinced, not from one source, but from many, that they would not dare say it was carelessness on his part. I am

personally much more willing to take the word of the mother, the father and the wife -that is three people-of the prisoner that the body was in a most disgraceful condition, than 1 am to believe those who said that it was embalmed. The government may have paid for the embalming and it may never have been done. From another letter which I have under my hand and which was also smuggled out, there is a very significant statement by the man to the effect that if you compared Stony Mountain with Portsmouth, Portsmouth was heaven and one lived there like a king. That is the opinion of the whdle gang of men who go from Portsmouth to Stony Mountain. But going back to this particular case, has the minister anyone else that he can quote as proving that the body was in good condition, other than the warden of Stony Mountain penitentiary whose statement does not prove anything?

,Progressive,,Agnes Campbell Macphail,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1d6a8f18-7d15-4909-b0f5-88f9b514f20a&Language=E&Section=ALL

886399,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.92,1929-06-12,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,There are two or three statements which are contained in the report of the superintendent of penitentiaries to which I should like to call attention. There is, I believe, a resident population of some 2,500 people, and the cost per capita is SI.50 per diem. I would simply point out that this involves a very heavy expenditure to the country at large, and that the actual cost of maintaining a criminal is much heavier than the cost of educating a child. It is much more expensive to keep those people in the penitentiary than to keep them from getting into it. I have been reading the record of one particular individual and the statement is made:
It might well be asked how such men as these came to be admitted to Canada.
I would refer that to the Minister of Immigration. When the superintendent of penitentiaries calls the attention of the country to the fact that we are bringing in very
Supply-Justice
undesirable immigrants, such cases ought to be carefully checked up and made the basis of very stringent regulations. Further on in the report this statement is made:
Another man about to be discharged wrote:-

When I came to prison I did not know anything. 1 was never given a chance, never was at school, could neither read nor write. I was not fitted for anything. I am going home with a fair education, am an expert blacksmith and also a good shoemaker. I have been taught both these trades in the penitentiary.""

This is undoubtedly very satisfactory from (he standpoint of the penitentiary, but I ask: Are we going to go along, year after year, spending $1.50 a day in training these people in blacksmithing and other trades when we refuse to help in anything like a scheme of technical education? I do not want to go into the question of technical education today except to point out that these matters are very closely related. If we deliberately refuse to train boys in their youth, we shall have to pay the bill later on in connection with the untrained men who go to the penitentiary. It seems to me again that these departments of our public life should be more closely correlated. Another paragraph in the report signed by General Hughes reads:

There should be some definite and properly organized endeavour, either by the Dominion or provincial governments, or both, to provide for the unfortunate dependents left behind when the wage-earner of a household is sentenced to prison. The leaving of a poor mother, frequently with several small children, without any means of support or chance of obtaining a livelihood, would seem a greater crime than very often is committed by the one who had been their provider. For long years the policy of ""the innocent must suffer for the sins of the guilty"" has ruled. Surely in the enlightened twentieth century this should not longer be regarded as a sufficient reason for leaving innocent mothers and children to starvation or worse.

Several years ago, after having debated this question during, I think, two distinct sessions, the house passed a resolution to the effect that payment should be made to the prisoners for work done in the penitentiary, and that in the case of married men, this amount should be turned over to their wives and children. The minister has apparently taken no action on that resolution. Again we ask:
column2: What about

column1: the responsibilities of the government to the house? The question was canvassed backwards and forwards very thoroughly: expert opinion was given as to what had been done and as to the beneficial results in other places. Nevertheless, year after year has passed and we have nothing done. I cannot conceive of a much more severe indictment of our present system than that from

the superintendent when he says that the crime committed against the prisoner or his dependents is often much more serious than that which the prisoner himself has committed. We cannot veiy well pass over these things year after year and have nothing done. This very significant statement is the last one made by the superintendent:
The recommendations made in former years are again suggested.

I would like to ask why we appoint a superintendent, expect him to make reports and then fail to act upon them. The superintendent does not even give the recommendations again this year. He apparentlj' feels it is hopeless to do so. They are not even put down in black and white. It would seem as if he was tired of making reports to the government, because the government passes over them. Most hon. members are not tremendously concerned over the penitentiary population. Most of us are trying to avoid this institution; we do not expect to go there. What do we care for a few criminals? The only opportunity we have in the house of discussing these matters is when we have the estimates before us, sometimes just a few hours before parliament prorogues. I would urge that the action of the bar associations and other bodies such as the Social Service Council, indicate that at least those who pay attention to this matter are heartily in sympathy with reforms along the line suggested by the superintendent of penitentiaries. It is due to the house that the Minister of Justice should tell us very definitely why he has not carried out the recommendations of the superintendent.

It is going to cost a good deal of money, but we are going to have the institutions, and even if I have only that to my credit during my administration of thei Department of Justice I shall be proud of it.

As far as the other matter is concerned, we must first of all have productive work that will bring in some return before we can divide the profits. We must first have the profits. The work done in the penitentiaries has been increasing year by year. We have installed new machinery, and to-day instead of the convicts merely breaking stones, most of the prisoners in the penitentiraies are working at some productive work. For a large number of years, of course, organized labour was opposed to prison labour coming into competition with their own, but now they have reached the stage where, although they do not want the products of prison labour to come into competition with the products of industry in the country they are willing that the departments of the government should buy such articles as they require which can be obtained from the penitentiaries. We have already started doing that to a certain extent, but I must remind my hon. friends that 1 am not in control of all the departments, and there will be some educational process necessary before I can convince all my colleagues that the products of the penitentiaries will meet their requirements as well as the work which is being produced by the ordinary industries of tlhe country.

I wish to say that in no country in the world are the prisoners paid anything before the expenses are met. The dtate certainly has the right to be reimbursed for the very large expenditure which is made to keep the penitentiaries working to maintain the prisoners in the penitentiaries. The only place I know of where anything is paid to the dependents of the convicts is in Minnesota. In some other places the system has been tried and abandoned periodically according to the changing views of the different governments coming into office. I have myself looked'into the records of what is being paid in some of the penitentiaries, and I find that in most of them nothing is being paid. In others an amount is paid varying from li cents-the rate paid in the big penal institutions in New York State-to 25 and even 50 cents a day. But as I stated, the expenses must first be met. When a convict is guilty of some offence against the regulations of the penitentiary a fine is imposed, and it is paid out of the little amount which may be to his
TMr. Lapointe.]

credit. However, even if it is impossible to collect something which might go to the dependents, and I find many difficulties in the way, we might at least provide a little amount for the prisoner when he has finished serving his sentence and is thrown out on the world. As it is to-day, he goes out with a suit of clothes and five dollars in his pocket, and a ticket to the place where he came from when admitted to the penitentiary. I think myself that it would be a great thing if they had some little amount to start with, although I must admit that the opinions of responsible people in places where that has been tried are that in many cases within two days after they have left the penitentiary, the amount is spent.

I said last year that I intended to visit all the penitentiaries in the country in the fall, but unfortunately, as my leader was sent to the League of Nations at the request of everybody in Canada, I had to stay in Ottawa at the very time when I wanted to make that visit, but I shall certainly visit the penitentiaries this year. Though I am willing to do anything I can in order to facilitate what I may call the reform of the convicts, rather than adhering to the old idea of punishment, and punishment alone, we must not go to the opposite extreme. Under the law he was now sent from the prison in Alberta to the Prince Albert penitentiary in Saskatchewan, which serves for the two provinces, and some time after he had been admitted to the penitentiary the surgeon of that institution certified that he had had this inmate under close observation since he had been admitted and found him to be insane, and he expressed the opinion that the man was insane when admitted. There is a section of the Penitentiary Act which I think I should read now that this matter is under discussion. Section 53 of that act reads:

If at any time within three months after the receipt at the penitentiary of any convict sentenced to imprisonment therein it is established to the satisfaction of the minister, either . by the written certificate of the surgeon of such penitentiary or otherwise, that the convict is insane or imbecile and was insane or imbecile at the time when he was received at the penitentiary, the minister may, after giving reasonable notice of his intention to the attorney general of the province within which such insane or imbecile convict was convicted, by warrant under his hand, direct the removal of such insane or imbecile convict from the penitentiary to the jail or other place of confinement from which such insane or imbecile convict came to the penitentiary.

Another section of the act provides that when, in the case of a prisoner who has been sentenced to death, such sentence is commuted to imprisonment for life, he shall be admitted to the penitentiary as though the order in council granting the commutation were a judgment of the court. Upon the receipt of this written certificate of the surgeon that Jackson was insane, we notified the attorney general of Alberta, under the section I have just read, on October 12, 1928, well within the three months provided for by statute, acquainting him with these facts; and we requested him to advise us as to which of the mental diseases hospitals the man might be taken to. We did not get an answer for some time and then we were told that, Jackson having been found sane by the jury at the trial, we should not have acted as we had done under the section of the statute to which I have referred. In view of this attitude on the part of the attorney general oif Alberta, I took upon myself to send an impartial medical expert from another province, Dr. MaoNeill of the mental hospital of North Battleford. Dr. MaoNeill is a well known authority, and he forwarded to us his report to the effect that the man was insane and that he could not understand how he had ever been sent to gaol. We again notified the authorities in Alberta and, upon their refusal to act, the officers of the peniten-
tiary proceeded upon the warrant which had been issued, taking the man to the prison in Alberta from which he had come.

They still claim that the man is sane, and I received' the day before yesterday a wire from Mr. Brownlee, in the absence of the attorney general, stating that they have had the man examined by four medical experts from Alberta, two from Edmonton, I believe, one from Calgary and one from some other place. These men say that the man is sane.

I do think that every facility should be offered by the institution for these men to better their education. I suppose that examinations are necessary, but I sometimes wonder whether we are not examination mad. But at least it is an advance over a few years ago.

One other thing. I think there should be an adjustment board to look after the man or woman when he is ready for release from the penitentiary. It should be composed, I think, of an official of the government of the institution, and outside civilians. The Red Cross has been built up by people who were not paid for doing it but who loved humanity sufficiently to give to give their time in its service. I think the same idea could be carried out with an adjustment board for each penitentiary. I have been very interested in half a dozen cases. Suppose a person has been in the penitentiary for five years and then comes out; there is no one to help adjust him to life again. They have this little bit of money, $5, and a suit of clothes, which I do not suppose is a very good suit, although it may be, and a railway ticket to take them ""uaiik where they came from. If any of us had been confined to this house for five years with no opportunity of getting out, and were turned out at the end of that time under such conditions, we might find a great deal of difficulty in adjusting ourselves. I think the superintendent would bear me out, if he could speak on the floor of the house, that it frequently happens that shortly after his release and before he gets to work again, reestablishes himself, and is absorbed again as

a human being into the human family, when everybody's hand is against him, the former prisoner becomes a repeater. That conditions in the world are not too good was proved by the words of the Minister of Justice today. It was a sad indictment of civilization to say that if the penitentiaries were made too comfortable and if the prisoners' dependents were looked after by the government, people would deliberately get into the penitentiaries. I cannot believe that people would deliberately give up their freedom for a period of years unless conditions were very bad outside.

I want to put on Hansard the recommendations of the superintendent of penitentiaries, W. S. Hughes, one of which is being carried out this year by the Minister of Justice. The recommendations are as follows:

column2: The providing of institutions for the segregation and classification of all inmates is again strongly recommended.
The reopening of the criminal mental disease hospital.

column1: The need for that is shown by the Jackson case.

column2: The segregation of habitual criminals.
The furnishing of more work for the inmates by the government.
Payment of wages to well-behaved inmates for work well performed.
The securing of situations for inmates prior to discharge.

column1: That is what I mean by an adjustment board. It is simply putting it in another way.

column2: The training of officers before being permitted to take charge of inmates.
The empowering of those in charge of penitentiary administration with authority to administer and discipline on similar basis to that of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

column1: I am not sure that I agree with the latter recommendation.

column2: Change in the method of purchasing supplies. This essential in order to attain success in the manufacture of goods in the penitentiaries.

column1: There is not any use at all in the superintendent of penitentiaries recommending to us again and again what he out of his experience has learned unless we are willing to take his expert advice and try a little more rapidly than we have been doing to carry out his recommendations. 886531,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.224,1929-06-12,17d9fbdf-1bc5-4137-ac59-4e782464990f,ca.m.4762,Mr. ROSS (Kingston):,,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,"Last session I proposed to the minister that in addition to getting this building and segregating these cases there should be also some examination of the boys to ascertain what started them on their criminal career. As I pointed out last year, there are some eight thousand juvenile delinquents in the Dominion of whom forty-six have now reached the penitentiary, some at the age of fifteen, others seventeen and eighteen. In my opinion there should be an investigation into the causes leading to this state of affairs; such an investigation could very well be made in the penitentiaries. The causes that have led to these forty-six boys finding themselves in the penitentiary would probably explain the delinquency of others. I hope that the minister will look into the matter. Now that this building is to be put up some steps should be taken in the direction I suggest. Last year I also pointed out the fallacy which prevails that these juvenile delinquents are for the most part foreigners; the fact is that they are Canadian born. I pointed out that delinquency had increased from 64 to 66 per cent, these delinquents having occurred amongst boj's who had not reached the higher stage of education. Surely something can be done in the way of investigating into the causes that have led to their condition.

886569,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.6.4.262,1929-06-12,4d5012f1-c091-43d5-b8fc-f6f7ac8afb9c,ca.m.491,Mr. LAPOINTE:,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,SUPPLY-TIME OF MEETING OF PARLIAMENT,DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE,,I think' I have already

explained this matter, but I have no objection to saying again that the Minister of National Revenue, as has been stated, sent to the Department of Justice the documents and the record with regard to this special case as well as those concerning many other cases. The offence charged had been committed in 1920. On the facts a prosecution might be entered, although the evidence was contradictory, with three witnesses on one side and three on the other. The offence was under the Customs Act, for having attempted to bribe officers in order to prevent them from stopping trucks which were coming from the United States to Canada, not for the purpose of smuggling goods into Canada but rather for the purpose of smuggling liquor from Canada into the United States. There is a provision in the Customs Act which compels any such trucks or motor cars to report to the Canadian customs when they enter Canada, and when that is not done the car is liable to seizure. The Customs Act provides also that any attempt to bribe a customs officer for the purpose of preventing him from doing his duty is an indictable offence subject to a penalty of fine and imprisonment. However, under another section of that act the prosecution must be instituted within three years after the commission of the offence. In this case the offence, as I have stated, was committed in 1920 and came to the notice of the Minister of National Revenue only as a result of the investigation of 1927, seven years
afterwards. Therefore the law officers came to the conclusion that this man should not be prosecuted under the provisions of the act, because of the statute of limitations. That is all.

was being urged on the farmers of Canada undoubtedly a great deal of grain, horses, cattle and implements were purchased for the Indians on the reserves. Unfortunately I have been selected to clean up the mess. I have been forced to this conclusion, that in every case where the creditor is able to produce an order we are in duty bound to pay the account. We have paid all that it was possible to pay out of the band funds available. I was in hopes that these accounts had been pretty nearly all cleaned up, except those still in dispute as to whether the transaction took place. One of the principles we insist upon is that we will not recognize now, and we have not for the past two years, any transaction with an Indian unless the creditor can produce an order signed by the agent. In every case where he is able to produce such an order we are prepared to settle, and in some cases where the evidence is clear that the transaction actually took place and that the creditor has given value for the claim, we will try to make an adjustment.

,Liberal,,Charles A. Stewart,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b&Language=E&Section=ALL
886643,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.9.3,1929-06-12,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR,,,Only one observation I have to make and that is as to the destitution of the Eskimos in remote sections of the country. I brought the matter to the attention of the government last year, and I may say that the Rev. W. G. Walton, with whom the minister has been in communication, is very anxious that it shall receive consideration by parliament. His view is that a large

number of people are suffering privation and practically starvation by reason of the lack of food, and that they might have their condition greatly improved if provision were made for reindeer. Before we rose at six o'clock the minister had not made any general statement as to the intention of the government in that regard and perhaps he will do so now, especially in view of the fact that there is some talk of establishing a beaver farm in a distant section of the country. The transportation difficulties would be considerable, hawing regard to the point of location and the distance between such a farm and the Eskimos. This reverend gentleman is of the opinion that if reindeer were introduced and looked after these people would not run the risk of starvation.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL

The missionary is stationed on the east coast of Hudson bay and the bands in that vicinity have experienced considerable difficulty. This year we are sending an officer to an island up there-I have foigotten the name-where application has been made for a beaver farm. He will investigate the possibilities and we hope we shall be able to provide sufficient food for these people. It is expected eventuality to give the Eskimo families a certain number of reindeer to provide them with meat, clothing and milk. With regard to the introduction of reindeer into the east of the delta of the Mackenzie river I shall be glad to give information later on in connection with the supplementaries as to what we are paying. We propose to have them driven across from Alaska and landed in Canada before we pay for them.

886689,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.9.49,1929-06-12,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Edmonton):,Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior,DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR,,,Yes, and they have day schools as well, carried on in tents located where the Eskimos are fishing in the summer season; but as in the Indian work, much better results can be obtained by boarding schools.

,Progressive,,Milton Neil Campbell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=06b3ede1-7cd7-46e9-87f5-23c426b95e96&Language=E&Section=ALL
886691,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.9.51,1929-06-12,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Edmonton):,Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior,DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR,,,We are told by our own officers who visit the Arctic that the arming of the Eskimo perhaps has not been altogether a good thing. Formerly when he missed a seal that seal was left alive, but now when he shoots a seal it often reaches a hole in the ice through which it gets back to the water and of course is not recoverable. The Eskimo is perhaps a little bit more clever than the ordinary northern Indian. He becomes an expert shot; he is a persistent hunter; he follows the game and builds his own home wherever night overtakes him, but in spite of that he may experience just a little more difficulty in obtaining a livelihood, and of course it is not good for him to attempt to live on the food of the white man, which usually brings illness. On the whole, the Eskimo is a very apt pupil; he learns quickly; he is of a mechanical turn of mind and will adapt himself to new conditions very rapidly, I think much more so than his Indian brother.

886693,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.9.53,1929-06-12,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Edmonton):,Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior,DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR,,,That idea is quite prevalent amongst the Eskimos, because they lead a nomadic life. The game in the north, as well as in the southern and western parts of the country, seems to enjoy periods of fairly large production; then they move to other sections, their numbers are greatly diminished and they have an off season. I think that has engendered in the minds of the Eskimos the idea that perhaps these animals will come back, but there is ample evidence that the musk-ox has been much farther south than we find it now. There is a considerable herd1 of musk-ox cm Ellesmere island but it was found that large parties were coming across from Greenland and slaughtering the animals. We have established posts there to stop that kind of thing, and although we have no definite information we believe that the herds are increasing.

886695,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.9.55,1929-06-12,022a8c13-6073-4481-8b89-af00b63bd91b,ca.m.9249,Mr. STEWART (Edmonton):,Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior,DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR,,,That has

been the main idea of introducing the reindeer. The history of Greenland under the administration of the Danish government shows that the reindeer has been the salvation of the northern peoples in that country. We propose to introduce the reindeer into our northern territories so that the Eskimo may be supplied with food and clothing as the farmer on the prairie obtains like supplies from his sheep or cattle, and we believe in that way the Eskimo will be taught the necessity of preserving game. As a rule the Eskimo and the Indian do not slaughter the game. It is the white man who is the vandal and who destroys the wild animals; he takes all the pelts he can gather without any thought as to reproduction.

886856,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.19,1929-06-12,ee1cc492-9867-48d3-a612-c1fb491d2916,ca.m.1883,Mr. WOODSWORTH:,,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,There is a question I should like to ask under this item, and I might say I brought to the attention of the department a case which illustrates my point. A judge in my own city sent in a report with regard to certain applications for naturalization, in which he stated that the applicants had not a sufficient knowledge of English. 886857,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.20,1929-06-12,d5513859-e07e-4492-ae07-70bda3037018,ca.m.1957,Mr. RINFRET:,Secretary of State of Canada,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,I have looked into a number of cases similar to the one mentioned by the hon. member. He is not quite right when he says that although a second report was made the department is adhering to the first one. When the famous bill concerning naturalization was before the house last year, I think I explained that although an applicant may come before the court we also conduct an

inquiry through the mounted police and the other means at the disposal of the department. In certain cases the report of the court is favourable while that of our inspectors is in the other direction, and it is within the discretion of the minister either to grant or to refuse the certificate. We do not act against the report of the court, but we do not always follow that recommendation, as sometimes we are not as easily satisfied as the tribunal has been. There is no finality to our decision, as the intervention of an influential person will induce us to renew our investigation in an effort to find out whether or not we have been misinformed.

886858,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.21,1929-06-12,06b3ede1-7cd7-46e9-87f5-23c426b95e96,ca.m.4681,Mr. CAMPBELL:,,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,I should like to draw the minister's attention to what seems to me to be somewhat of an anomaly in the Naturalization Act. I have in my hand a file covering the case of Mr. H. Stuckenberg, who is living at the present time at Kandahar, in Saskatchewan. Mr. Stuckenberg was a Danish citizen but had lived in Canada for a number of years. He enlisted in the army at the outbreak of the war and took the oath of allegiance at that time. Apparently that destroyed his Danish citizenship, because when he attempted to obtain a passport to visit his native country he found that he was not a Danish citizen, and he also discovered that he was not a Canadian citizen. Here is a man who took upon himself the supreme obligation of citizenship; he enlisted in the army and served throughout the whole war. I have discussed this case with the deputy minister and it has been pointed out to me that under the present legislation this man is not a citizen. Of course the minister can reply that he should make application for naturalization in the ordinary way, but this man thinks that that would be humiliating, and I agree with him. He does not feel that he should be forced to appear before the clerk of the court, pay about ten or fifteen dollars in lawyers' fees and other expenses, :and go through all the formality of becoming .a Canadian citizen. I suggest to the minister that seme change should be made in the act which would admit a man of that type to citizenship.

886863,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.26,1929-06-12,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,I think the bon. gentleman is under a misapprehension. Under our present act naturalization depends upon two things; (a) residence and (b) character, habits and reputation. Service under the colours does not constitute residence because a man may become a soldier and yet not be a citizen. Taking the oath of allegiance merely means that he takes it to serve in that capacity. The difficulty in meeting the suggestion of the hon. gentleman is that this is an imperial act in the sense that in granting a certificate of naturalization we do not confer Canadian citizenship; we confer British citizenship which is good the world over. If we amend our statute it must be amended in all the overseas dominions and in Great Britain as well, because we have adopted a uniformity of qualification in order to confer a uniform citizenship. I have had to deal with more than one case of a similar nature, and there seems to be a misunderstanding on the part of those who took the oath of allegiance; it is an oath to serve the country in the capacity of a soldier, and not an oath of citizenship or naturalization,^ which involves a further inquiry upon which the granting of the certificate is predicated.
Mr. CAMPBELL; I quite understand that the man is not a citizen under the present act.

,Liberal,,Louis Édouard Fernand Rinfret,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d5513859-e07e-4492-ae07-70bda3037018&Language=E&Section=ALL
886869,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.32,1929-06-12,06b3ede1-7cd7-46e9-87f5-23c426b95e96,ca.m.4681,Mr. CAMPBELL:,,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,Let me remind the

minister of a phase of this matter which I have discussed many times before. There are in my constituency many people of foreign birth-and this would apply all over Canada -who find it very inconvenient to go to the judicial centres and appear before a judge to make their application for naturalization.

On many branch lines there is only a triweekly service, and it means a week away from home. Many of these settlers are very poor; the 125 to S30 it would cost them means a great deal, and many people are going without naturalization simply because they cannot afford it. I have suggested both to the minister and to his deputy that arrangements should be made so that the judges could hear these cases when they are sitting at local points. The deputy minister promised me that something would be done, and in some cases this arrangement has been made. In my own village of Pelly, where the judge sits once a year, there have been a few cases dealt with in this way, but at other times this procedure is not earned out. In most cases the judges refuse to deal with the applicants at that local point, and the people living in the local district where the judge comes once, twice or sometimes three times a year, have to go to all the trouble and expense of travelling to the judicial centre, and this means a considerable expense. The Under Secretary of State pointed out to me that this could be arranged only by cooperation with the provincial authorities. Apparently no provision is made for extra expenses of the judges when this would entail remaining over in the district for another day. I want to suggest to the minister that this matter be further discussed with the provincial authorities. There is no reason in the world why proper arrangements could not be made so that these cases could be dealt with at every local point, thus saving these people all the delay, trouble and expense of going to the judicial centre.

,Progressive,,Milton Neil Campbell,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=06b3ede1-7cd7-46e9-87f5-23c426b95e96&Language=E&Section=ALL
886870,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.33,1929-06-12,d5513859-e07e-4492-ae07-70bda3037018,ca.m.1957,Mr. RINFRET:,Secretary of State of Canada,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,My hon. friend is aware, as I reminded him a moment ago, that the best way to deal with t'he situation he has depicted would have been for both houses of parliament to adopt a bill which I introduced last year to do away altogether with appearance before a court. This house assented to the bill by a somewhat large majority, but it failed to pass the other house, and therefore the amendment which we sought and for which I fought rather energetically, did not become law. We do not have any power over the judges, as my hon. friend will appreciate. The act provides that the applicant shall go before a tribunal, and we are powerless to compel either the clerk of the court or the judge himself to deal with the cases sooner or in some other manner than that which the judge himself determines. We are doing everything in our power by negotiation and conciliation to expedite the work of the appli-

886875,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.38,1929-06-12,0e1575e1-8782-4de1-8bdb-742a2019685e,ca.m.724,Mr. WARD:,,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,I am not sure whether this

is the proper place to suggest amendments to the Naturalization Act, but I should like to suggest a modification of that law, which, as it stands at present, compels all new Canadians to have a working knowledge, so to speak, of the English or the French language before being permitted to become naturalized Canadian citizens. In this connection we should take into consideration the fact that a large number of new Canadians come to Canada in middle life with no knowledge of either English or French, but immediately

become good Canadian citizens and endeavour to educate their families. In fact I have in my constituency many families where the parents cannot speak a word of English but where some of the children have taken the highest honours in the universities. New Canadians who are endeavouring to live up to all the laws of Canadian society, who are just as good citizens as those who speak our languages, should not be debarred from becoming Canadian citizens because they cannot speak the English or the French language. A grave injustice has been done to many new Canadians by the fact that under the circumstances under which they were placed In (his country, they cannot become naturalized citizens. We all know that the policy of settlement, whether it was right or wrong, has isolated those people in the west. For instance, one district will be German, another Austrian, another something else, and they have principalities of their own with no opportunity of learning the English language. Persons who come here from other lands in middle life, therefore, and who are anxious to become good Canadians, should not be debarred from securing naturalization simply because they cannot speak the English or the French language.

called to one particular incident that may give point to what has just been said. An elderty Icelandic woman came to this country some years ago and moved up country between lake Manitoba and lake Winnipeg. She lived a hard life under those pioneering conditions, brought up her family there, contributed as much as she possibly could to the upbuilding of this country. She was in every way an intelligent woman, but she had no opportunity, in that isolated life, of learning another language. The question of old age pensions came up. 886916,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.79,1929-06-12,f88a7275-f7f4-407e-9d45-89d5300f2919,ca.m.9510,Mr. POULIOT:,,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,Unfortunately there is no radio in this house so that my speech cannot be heard in Hull to-night. Now it is rather hard to expect a supporter of the provincial government to move a vote of censure against that government; but how could it be explained that matters of such great importance have not been brought before the Quebec legislature by any member of the provincial opposition, not even by the Conservative members of Montreal? What is this or that piece of their criticism compared to the welfare and comfort of so many large families?
Taking the official report of the Dominion-provincial conference held in 1927, I find that the Premier of Quebec is reported thus:

Premier Taschereau, of Quebec, declared at the outset that he was not asking for anything at all for his province. He was surprised that after all the conferences which had been held, and after sixty years of partnership, there should still be so much friction between the provinces and the Dominion as to their respective domains. To have a happy and prosperous Canada there must be happy and prosperous provinces, and the latter could do more for Canada than could the federal authorities. The provinces were more in contact with the people, educating them, building their roads, and looking after their health. The provinces enacted compensation laws in favour of workmen and had control of the judicial machinery.
He was not asking for anything at all for his province!"" Wliat about federal subsidies to the provinces for highways and so many

other purposes, including public works and so forth? What about his own request, on behalf of his Siamese brother, Sir Herbert Holt, for the disappearance of the income tax, against the recommendations of the labour congress? What about his own requests of millions to dredge the St. Charles river and to build Canadian National railway terminals at Quebec?

The provinces would do more for Canada than would the federal authorities."" What about the reduction of the debt of this country and the general reduction of the burden of taxation, the extension of our domestic and foreign trade, the settlement of labour troubles, the wonderful work done by federal research experts and civil servants, the policy of this government in regard to imperial matters, and so forth? I quote from the Montreal Gazette of January 10, 1928:

In introducing a large delegation of the trades and labour congress of Canada, Mr. Tom Moore, the chairman, took occasion to compliment the (federal) government upon its labour legislation. He particularly approved the government's old age pension scheme and asked that any changes which the government might see fit to introduce which would make easier the acceptance of the measure by some of the provinces would be welcomed. The government was also commended for its enactment of the Trade Mark and Designs Act, which now enables the labour organizations to register and probably protect their union labels, etc.

The congress also noted with satisfaction the treaty of the Canadian National^ Steamships giving effect to their recommendations for the carrying on of the West Indies service by a government owned line in cooperation with the Canadian National Railways; the act amending t'he Workmen's Compensation Aot respecting government employees; amendments to the income tax; the acts encouraging the use of Canadian mined coal and others.

He was not asking anything at all for his province!"" Such a proud declaration does not prevent the federal government from taking every possible means to help our province, as well as the sister provinces, against his will. But although the artisan who receives fair wages does not require so badly the help of the state as the one who is insufficiently paid, although the artisans of the province of Quebec are the least remunerated in the Dominion, and although the five sister provinces of British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario have already accepted the old age pension scheme, he for instance even refusees any assistance from the federal government in that connection.
I am happy to congratulate the Minister of Labour upon having gone yesterday to
Supply-Labour
Toronto by airplane to sign the old age pension contract with the representatives of the provincial government of Ontario.

In that momentous gathering of the official representatives of the federal and provincial governments, speaking on behalf of his province, he said that he was not asking for anything at all for his province. Was that declaration criticized by the provincial opposition? No; it was approved by them. I have as much personal regard for Mr. Sauve, the leader of the Quebec opposition, as for Mr. Taschereau, and I do not understand how he would have unreservedly praised the attitude of the Quebec premier at the Dominion-provincial conference. In fact, two months afterwards, he concluded his speech on the address with these words:

The Prime Minister at this conference took a part which honoured his province, his government and his race. I say this to render justice to him, even at the risk of drawing upon myself reproaches and not figuring in the least that the Prime Minister will long remember my expression of sentiment.
This is f-rom The Gazette, Montreal, January, 13, 1928.
It is to be noted that Mr. Sauve has never been censured by his followers for such a declaration.

Evidently no blame can be put on the federal authorities for the difficulties and low wages of labour in the province of Quebec. As the situation of labour is satisfactory in most of the other provinces, why is it not so in Quebec? What is the local cause of such unfair treatment? Why does capital enjoy there such excessive earnings at the expense of labour? The astonishing and appalling figures that have been given call for immediate relief and for the kind consideration of the best friend of labour amongst labour men in this country. I mean our active and competent Minister of Labour (Mr. Heenan), who himself comes from the ranks of labour.

May I quote some clippings from the press in regard to the activities of the Minister of Labour since he has been in office? The following is from the Toronto Star, as quoted by the Ottawa Citizen, June, 29, 1927:

Canada's act making an attempt at conciliation before the declaration of a strike or lockout was torpedoed by a verdict of the privy council. The damage thus done may not be serious if the Dominion always has a Minister of Labour as earnest and as persistent as Peter Heenan in seeking to maintain industrial peace.
Then in the Brockville Recorder of November 10, 1927, I find the following:
Following other triumphs in the settlement of labour troubles, he has been successful in
bringing peace in the Toronto building trades and has thus earned the gratitude and the congratulations of the mayor of that city, no small achievement for any member of any Liberal ministry.
Then, in the Sydney Record of November 25, 1927, appeared this statement:

He is useful and successful because lie knows the labour problems from the labour point of view and because, at the same time, he has an equipment of mind and character which makes him fair and reasonable in dealing with capital.
Again from the Sydney Record:

They (Premier Rhodes and his ministers) haven't brought about -a satisfactory settlement of the present coal wage dispute, and if settlement comes it will be as a result of the intervention of Hon. Peter Heenan, federal Minister of Labour, who had to come info the case because of the failure of Hon. G. S. Harrington to bring the operators and miners to terms.
Then I quote from the Halifax Citizen of December 2, 1927:

He is a labour man and appears to be a real live wire with the right idea of getting into personal touch with labour all over Canada. His splendid work for old age pensions, his services in the Toronto strike, and his visit to the industrial centres of Nova Scotia, all give promise of better service from the department in the future.
Then I quote from the Oshawa Daily Times of March 31, 1928:

In our opinion great credit is due to the Minister of Labour for coming to Oshawa in person and lending his good offices to bring about a settlement of the strike. His arrival here yesterday was, in our opinion, most opportune, and his wise counsel and fair dealing was, we believe, appreciated by both parties to the controversy. The people of Oshawa will have a higher opinion of Peter Heenan as a result of his visit here this week.

Then I quote from the Saskatoon Star of May 25, 1929:
Peace In Industry

Another factor in recent years has been the skill of Hon. Peter Heenan, the Dominion Minister of Labour, in conciliating workers and employees who fall out over wages, working conditions and recognition of unions. The latest illustration of Mr. Heenan's capacity as an arbiter of such disputes is his settlement of the plumbers' and steamfitters' strike in Toronto. This strike, according to the Toronto Globe, was peculiarly difficult to handle but the minister did the trick by calling a round table conference of the parties to the dispute. Once again, the Globe remarks, he lived up to his name as ""Peter the Peacemaker"".
Then I quote from the Fort William Times Journal of December 9, 1927:

He has seen the labour situation from the workers' sid-e. ... As an experienced labour man, he knows that trouble is best dealt with when it is caught in the bud, instead of being left to ripen to the full fruit. Hence comes his desire to leave behind him the reputation, as Minister of Labour, of having prevented more strikes than he settled.
Now I quote from the Port Arthur Chronicle of the same date:

It is Mr. Heenan's job to take a large share in making conditions contentful for the wage earners of the Dominion. . . . No Minister of Labour has applied himself to the work of the department over which he presides more assiduously than he.
My last quotation is from the Hamilton Labour World of May 30, 1929:

As Minister of Labour for the Dominion, Hon. Peter Heenan has made a name for himself in the settling of differences between employer and employee. The old arbitration board is a thing of the past, as has been manifested in the confidence placed in the ability of this stalwart to negotiate.

Strikes received short shift when the Hon. Mr. Heenan steps in, and he has established a record in early settlements when he gets into action. When everything fails, the human dynamo tabes hold to show both sides where they are wrong. His slogan is, ""Let nothing retard industry where reason should prevail.""

The long years at the throttle give him an experience which could not be duplicated, for there he had courage, conviction and ability. The workers of Canada may justly be proud of their representative in the Dominion parliament, and they are.

Since by virtue of the act respecting his department the Minister of Labour ""shall institute and conduct inquiries into important industrial questions, upon which adequate information may not at present be available"", would it be possible for him to intervene. in this case for the relief of the artisans of the province of Quebec?
I have just one further quotation to make; it is from the Brockville Recorder of December 9, 1927:

At a luncheon at Glace Bay in December, 1927, Mr. Heenan said to the representatives of the United Mine Workers of Cape Breton, ""I want you to feel that I am a public servant, and_ if you need me, just press the button and I will come.""

This is my point, Mr. Chairman: The products of Quebec are not sold at a lower price than the same products are sold by Ontario manufacturers, but the employees in Quebec are paid much les3. That means a lost to labour and an undue surplus of profit to the manufacturer. This is a very bad situation, and it is the reason why I thought it proper to-night, although we are at the close of the session, to ask the Minister of Labour to investigate that situation in the interests of the workers of that province.

Supply-Labour

since her appointment to this position. Of course there is no objection to a lady who is a Liberal being appointed to the position, any more than there would be objection to a lady who was a Conservative or a lady who represented the Progressive party or any other party, but this lady has a political record which is distinctly partisan. Not only was her previous political record so distinctly partisan, but since she received this appointment it has continued to be very partisan. I think the minister is to be criticized for not stopping her political activities after this appointment was made. This lady was president of the Liberal Association at British Columbia; she then became a member of the local legislature; she became a minister without portfolio; then she lost the confidence of the people of British Columbia to such an extent that she bad to change her ridiing, and she was defeated in the new riding. She then came to Ottawa and was appointed president of the ladies' Liberal federation of Canada-I think that is the name, but I am not sure. There is nothing wrong with all that, except that she had lost the confidence of the people of British Columbia and, therefore, I doubt if she has the confidence of the ladies of Canada. After having been appointed to this position she certainly lost the confidence of half the ladies of this country, those who are Conservatives, because she passed from one end of the country to the other making political speeches; she showed the bad taste of making political speeches after she had been given this appointment by the Minister of Labour.

After all, the League of Nations is an organization which we all wish to see succeed. It is non-political in every way and is an organization which all right-minded people desire to be of the greatest use to the world. A large proportion of the people of Canada have the desire to see the League of Nations successful, because it is an organization for the purpose of spreading peace throughout the world. That being the case, how can the Minister of Labour or the government expect a lady with such partisan political leanings to represent truly the women of Canada? How can they expect the women of all political persuasions in this country to take any interest in the League of Nations when a woman is appointed who has shown so much political partisanship after her appointment? She travelled one end of the country to the other making political speeches, and although I cannot prove my statement I have no doubt that she travelled at the expense of the government. I object, not as a Conservative,

but as a Canadian, to any representative of ours travelling under the aegis of the League of Nations and making political speeches. I object to her or any other representative of the people of Canada at the League of Nations making a political football out of that organization. I would like to get, and I think the committee should get from the Minister of Labour the absolute assurance that when this lady comes back her political activities will be stopped while she is more or lees in the pay of the people of Canada, because the government of this country is not a political party; the government represents the people of the country while it is in power, and she should be instructed by the Minister of Labour or by the government to keep away from any political partisanship when she is speaking to the people on the question of the League of Nations, until her appointment expires. Let her stick to the League of Nations and keep away from politics.
