Mr. Chairman, that there ought to be a much closer arrangement between the Department of Immigration and the employment agencies as operated under the Department of Labour.

I should like to read two or three paragraphs from a letter that I received about two months ago, simply because this very well illustrates the position in which a great many casual labourers find themselves in this country. The writer used to be in British Columbia; I knew him there some years ago. For a time he was a settler on a farm there. Then he says:
Owing 'to my wife's death our home in British Columbia was broken up and I went back to bush work, which I had followed up when I was a single man.

This fall I happened to be in Ofctawa^ after doing a summer's work in Ontario, working as navvy on the new highways. Well soon I was broke, had to go to work again. Engaged as general bushman at thirty-five dollars a month, board and bunk found, went down the Soo to work. Well when we goit there we found the camp full of Swedes. Started work November 5th and finished work January 30th. Well after paying train fare here and living expenses got a few needful lumbermen's clothes, etc., I was broke. Then I found myself in Port Arthur destitute, stone broke. So had to go to the police station. I asked the police officer if I was to commit a crime or what. I wanted the right to work to live. They said, commit no crime but come up and the magistrate will sentence you under charge of vagrancy-no visible means of support. I got two months at the industrial farm. There -fere several I found at the farm in the same boat, no work, but the farm. Well, I came out of the jail farm at Fort William this morning. The work there is all right, food and bunk good, but the disgrace of mixing up and being locked up with petty thieves, etc. Surely there can be something done better than jail hard-working men.
Then he comments on the cause of himself and other men being placed in this position, He says:

Now, as I said when I arrived at the Soo camp it was full of Swedes. We the Britishspeaking men were fired when the logs and roads were finished, the Swedes were kept on because they had been imported for twelve months' work, after the sleigh haul they were to start in the saw-mill. You see, sir, the timber companies know a thing or two about labour-every year they import green young men from Europe to atop the older men from organization to better thirty-five dollars a month, etc. So the new blood is kept on and the older bushmen take down the road. If broke we go to jail as vagrants.

I venture to read those paragraphs because in their own way, in not the very best English, they very well put the situation in which a great many casual labourers find themselves to-day. And we have to remember that a great deal of the construction work, bush work and harvest work across this country is carried on by these same transient labourers. It does seem that so long as there is a supply of these men in this country we have absolutely no right to admit any others. I think the labour department has a responsibility to insure that these men's jobs are protected. In this case the foreign-born men were given the preference, and men who had been for the greater part of their lives in this country were left jobless. tre is of very great importance to every person who is sympathetic to labour in Canada. Labour throughout this country is vitally interested in a reasonably short work day. I quite understand that this government cannot legislate for the provinces generally in the matter of the eight hour day, but certainly this government has the power to put in the eight hour day in connection with government work, and if my hon. friend the minister deserves a thousandth part of the eulogy, the panegyric and the bouquets flung at him tonight by the hon. member for Temiscouata he should give a lead to industrial corporations in this matter. To say that we will have it next session is merely to say that although he has been eulogized as the greatest Minister of Labour we have ever known he has fallen down on one of the most vital questions concerning organized and unorganized labour throughout Canada. There is absolutely no reason for delay in this matter. When workingmen try to obtain a reasonably short working day, one which will give them an opportunity for recreation, a chance to improve their mental faculties and sufficient rest, they are generally met with the statement that the government of this country itself asks its employees on its public works to work ten hours a day, at a wage of twenty-five cents an hour. That is the situation with regard to the construction of wharves and breakwaters in the maritime provinces. My hon. friend has mentioned the application of a fair wage clause. I want to ask the minister why it is that when the Department of Public Works starts to construct a wharf somewhere in the maritime provinces they always base what they call their fair wage clause on the rate prevailing in that district for unorganized labour. Why do they not take the rate which has been obtained by the organized workmen through collective bargaining? If we are to judge by the minister's reply to-night he hardly merits the very splendid and carefully prepared eulogy sung by the hon. member for Temiscouata. I do not think there should be any further delay in this matter; if my hon. friend is a real friend of labour, as I believe he is, he should use those powers which he possesses as Minister of Labour to see that organized and unorganized labour throughout Canada have a reasonably short work day. He can do it with respect to government contracts; the matter brooks no delay, and there is absolutely no shadow or semblance of an excuse for delay.

Early in the session I presented the plight of steel workers in Sydney who are working eleven hours by day and thirteen hours at night. They get one Sunday off in two weeks, and they make up for that by working on alternate fortnights for twenty-four hours on end. The salaries of the deputies is a troublesome question at all times. We have adopted a rule, which when I mention it, I 'think will be accepted. At all events that is the explanation. In every case where a deputy has served for ten years or moire, and is in active service at the head of the department, he receives the increase, unless he already has the increased salary; but as to the others there is no discrimination, except that which arises from the term of service.

The significance given to those words is attached to them in all the other statutes referring to them-the Superannuation Act, the Retirement Fund Act, the Insurance Act, and other acts. In other words, the definition given by the Civil Service Act is the definition that is accepted in the other statutes in dealing with various appointees. So that a discrimination has been practised with respect to a number of these gentlemen. In addition to that there is no fixed principle applied to those who are deputy ministers of departments. Mr. Fielding said it was difficult, but he laid down a rule. In this instance, as I pointed out the other day, if you take the various departments and go through

them you will see one deputy minister getting an increase of $1,000, another an increase of $2,000, another an increase of $1,800, and so on, without regard to any fixed principle that could be applied; and certainly with respect to one or two of them it is perfectly clear that their duties are very, very light, while in other cases they are very, very onerous. I take this opportunity of mentioning this because the other evening I mentioned the deputy of the Minister of National Defence, whose duties have become very much lighter because of the disarmament alleged by the minister, and the position of the Deputy Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to which reference was made the other evening. Now we come to the Department of Labour, in which I think there has been a departure from the principle laid down by Mr. Fielding in the first instance.

887121,ca.proc.d.1929-06-12.10.284,1929-06-12,d0fdc43a-2bf2-47f2-a4e7-5e122182e613,ca.m.1387,Mr. STEWART (Leeds):,,SECRETARY OF STATE,,,I should like also to refer to a statement made by the right hon. the Prime Minister in discussing the position of the chairman of the Civil Service Commission. He was under the impression that Doctor Roche simply held office for a fixed term and was not in the same position as a deputy minister. In the Civil Service Act of 1918, chapter 12, part 1, section 3, it is provided:

There shall be three commissioners each with the rank of a deputy minister. Each commissioner shall hold office during good behaviour, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.

Provided, however, that any commissioner hereafter appointed shall hold office during good behaviour for a period of ten years from the date of his appointment, but shall be removable by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons, and shall cease to hold office upon reaching the age of sixty-five years.
Then the Civil Service Act found in the present revised statutes, chapter 22, provides by subsection 3 of section 3:-

column2: The commissioners in office on the twenty-fourth day of May, one thousand nine hundred and eighteen, shall hold office during good behaviour. Each subsequently appointed commissioner hsall hold office during good behaviour cor a period of ten years from the date of his appointment, save that his tenure of office shall cease upon his attaining the age of sixty-five years.

column1: By subsection 4 it is provided:
Any commissioner shall be removed from office at any time by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
So that the head of the Civil Service Commission holds office for life, and not for a fixed period of ten years. He is in all respects in the same position as any deputy minister.
In fact, he is in a stronger position, I should think. It would appear that he ought to be treated in the same way as other deputy ministers.
